problem_type: Insect pest damage, not a plant disease

egypt_status.first_report: 2019 in Aswan Governorate, including Kom Ombo
egypt_status.egypt_research: Egyptian field studies have documented infestation on maize, yield impacts, seasonal generations, growth-stage susceptibility, and characteristic leaf and whorl damage.
egypt_status.important_scope_note: The term armyworm can refer to several caterpillar species. This Egypt-focused record uses fall armyworm, Spodoptera frugiperda, because it is the armyworm species specifically documented as an invasive maize pest in Egypt.

early_stage: Transparent elongated scraped patches or window-pane areas where young larvae feed on the leaf surface
Small shot holes after damaged leaves expand
Fine linear scratches or translucent streaks on young leaves
whorl_stage: Irregular elongated holes in newly emerging leaves
Clusters of holes and windowing concentrated in the central whorl
Wet or dry sawdust-like frass inside the whorl and around leaf axils
advanced_stage: Large irregular holes and torn leaf margins
Extensive loss of green photosynthetic tissue or leaf skeletonisation
Dead or torn central leaves, sometimes described as a damaged or dead heart
Holes or feeding injuries in stems in heavy infestations
Damage to tassels, silks, and ears at later growth stages
larval_visual_features: Caterpillars may be green, tan, brown, or nearly black depending on age and conditions
Head commonly shows a pale inverted Y-shaped marking
Four dark spots arranged approximately as a square can occur near the rear abdominal segments
Larvae hide deep in the whorl during the day and leave frass near feeding sites
image_annotation_targets: stem, silk, tassel, or ear feeding damage
visible larval head pattern and body markings

distribution_on_plant: Often concentrated in the central whorl and on newly expanding leaves, but older larvae may feed on outer leaves, stems, tassels, silks, ears, and kernels.
progression: Eggs hatch and young larvae scrape the leaf surface, producing translucent window panes.
As leaves expand, scraped areas appear as shot holes or elongated transparent patches.
Larger larvae feed deep in the whorl, producing irregular holes, ragged leaves, and frass accumulation.
Heavy whorl injury can kill the central growing point and cause a dead-heart or severely torn plant centre.
Later infestations can injure stems, tassels, silks, ears, and kernels and reduce grain yield.

egypt_field_evidence.nile_delta: A 2024 report documented fall armyworm as a new invasive pest on maize in the Nile Delta and noted its earlier Egyptian records in Aswan in 2019 and Assiut in 2021.
egypt_field_evidence.nubaria_beheira: Field experiments in Nubaria, Beheira, recorded five generations on maize from 1 May to 30 November in both study seasons.
egypt_field_evidence.yield_loss: Untreated Nubaria plots recorded quantitative grain-yield losses of 77.76% and 78.89% in the two study seasons; these are experiment-specific results, not a national average.
egypt_field_evidence.growth_stage: An Egyptian study found the late-whorl stage to be among the most susceptible stages, while mature plants had the lowest infestation rate.
egypt_field_evidence.seasonal_hybrid_evidence: A 2025 Egyptian study reported the highest infestation across tested hybrids in the 15 July sowing date, with SC-2088 showing the highest mean infestation among the evaluated hybrids.

environment.temperature_and_season: Warm maize-growing periods favour rapid development; Egyptian studies recorded activity from spring/summer through harvest, with infestations beginning around the third week of June in one field study.
environment.humidity: Humidity is not required to produce visible feeding injury, but rainfall, irrigation, and dense maize can influence egg survival, larval development, and plant attractiveness.
environment.crop_stage: Young maize through the whorl stage is particularly vulnerable; late-whorl plants can show severe central-leaf damage.
field_risk_factors: nearby infested maize or grassy hosts

similar_problems.name: Maize stem borer damage
similar_problems.visual_difference: Stem borers commonly produce entry holes, frass, and dead hearts, but fall armyworm characteristically produces window-pane feeding and ragged holes in the whorl.

similar_problems.name: Cutworm injury
similar_problems.visual_difference: Cutworms usually cut seedlings at or near the soil surface rather than producing extensive windowing deep in the maize whorl.

similar_problems.name: Hail, wind, or mechanical injury
similar_problems.visual_difference: Tearing may be widespread and random but normally lacks larvae, concentrated whorl feeding, and fresh frass.

similar_problems.name: Leaf-feeding beetles
similar_problems.visual_difference: Often create small round holes or edge feeding without the deep whorl injury and sawdust-like frass typical of fall armyworm.

diagnostic_caution: Do not identify fall armyworm from leaf holes alone. Inspect the whorl for larvae and frass, and examine larval markings when possible. Confirm species using morphological or molecular identification if regulatory or management decisions depend on the diagnosis.
